questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a 72-hour history of fever and malaise. He also had a mild headache and reported some loose stools and abdominal pain. He had returned 5 days earlier from a 6-week trip to Chad where he worked with locals to build a church. During the construction work, he was bitten by many mosquitoes. He also traveled throughout the region inspecting waterways. He had unprotected vaginal intercourse with 2 casual partners. He did not seek advice prior to his travels. On examination, his temperature was 39.3°C, his heart rate was 88 beats/minute, and his blood pressure was 120/68 mmHg. He was flushed with reddened conjunctivae. He had tender hepatomegaly of 2 cm below the costal margin. Investigations: Total WBC count 3.5 ×109/L Platelet count 150 ×109/L eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Bilirubin 3 mg/dL AST 177 U/L ALT 89 U/L
questions.lead_in: What intervention would have prevented his condition?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever immunization This is yellow fever, within the first viremic stage of infection. This will be followed by a period of remission for up to 48 hours, and then a proportion of patients will develop the third life-threatening stage of intoxication. Yellow fever vaccine is recommended for patients (above the age of 9 months) who will travel to the Americas and sub-Saharan Africa. This live attenuated vaccine is not recommended for immunocompromised patients. Booster doses after 10 years are recommended to a subset of individuals who may be at continued risk. Malaria, viral hepatitis, and leptospirosis should be considered in the differential but the rash, the platelet count, and the normal renal function make them less likely than yellow fever. Antibiotic or antiparasitic prophylaxis may be recommended on certain geographic regions, but would not protect him against yellow fever. Hepatitis A, typhoid, and hepatitis B immunizations would all be appropriate to recommend to this man, but would not have protected him.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q28

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man was admitted with new onset confusion and a 2-day history of fevers. The fevers began during his return home from a month-long safari in South Africa. He was found to have severe P. falciparum malaria and treated with IV artesunate with significant improvement. Ten days later, he developed a sudden drop in hemoglobin and rise in bilirubin.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Artesunate hemolysis Delayed postartesunate hemolysis is likely the result of the clearance of previously infected erythrocytes by the spleen. Artesunate kills parasites while not affecting the erythrocytes themselves; however, their ultimate lifespan is shortened. This generally happens 7–14 days after treatment initiation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q8

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man developed fever and headache 1 week after returning from an 8-week holiday to South America. He had stayed in a retreat in the middle of the Amazon jungle. He did not seek travel advice before his travel and had not taken any malaria prophylaxis or travel vaccinations. He had stayed in a wood hut with palm leaf roof. He slept under a bednet, but he ran out of mosquito repellent. He had been well while there. His symptoms had persisted for 4 days before he sought medical attention. A fellow traveler had informed him that she had been diagnosed with malaria. On examination he was alert and oriented. His heart rate was 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/74 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. He was thin, but there was no palpable lymphadenopathy or rash. Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal systems was unremarkable. Investigations: Hemoglobin 114 g/L (130–180) Platelet count 137 ×109/L (150–400) Serum creatinine 74 μmol/L (60–110) Malaria antigen positive Malaria film: see image
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine plus primaquine This is the recommended treatment of choice for P. vivax infection currently according to Public Health England. Primaquine is required to clear the hypnozoite stage of infection in order to prevent relapse. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)

Ten days earlier he had arrived in the United States from Myanmar. He had no prior medical history but had been depressed for the past year. On examination, he was awake, alert, and oriented. His temperature was 39.2°C, and his blood pressure was 110/58 mmHg. He had pale conjunctivae and some pitting edema to his ankles. questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by atovaquone– proguanil for 3 days
IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by oral mefloquine for 3 days
IV artesunate to complete 3-day course of therapy

questions.explanation: IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by atovaquone– proguanil for 3 days The peripheral smear shows the presence of a Plasmodium falciparum gametocyte, classically described as “bananashaped” and ring trophozoites. Although the patient is hemodynamically stable, he has signs of severe malaria, including a hemoglobin <7 g/dL and a bilirubin >3 mg/mL. For that reason, the most appropriate therapy is IV therapy with artesunate followed by an oral agent. The IV therapy should be continued for a minimum of 24 hours and should be transitioned to an oral regimen to complete a full course of therapy. They also need to have a second agent to ensure eradication of parasites. The patient has a prior history of depression and mefloquine would be contraindicated as it is associated with neuropsychiatric disturbances. Given the emergence of resistance in the South Asian continent, chloroquine is no longer an acceptable option for this region. (From Garcia LS. Malaria. Clin Lab Med. 2010;30(1):93–129.)

questions.model_answer:
a) Criteria met in this nonimmune traveller: (1) Cerebral malaria — impaired consciousness (GCS 9); (2) Respiratory distress/hypoxia — SaO2 85%; (3) Severe anaemia — Hb 65 g/L; (4) Hyperparasitaemia — P. falciparum 6% (any parasitaemia is dangerous in a nonimmune host).
b) Sequestration (cytoadherence) of P. falciparum–infected erythrocytes in the cerebral microvasculature; classically accompanied by ring haemorrhages.
c) Four other criteria: (1) prostration; (2) hypoglycaemia; (3) jaundice/icterus; (4) renal insufficiency (also shock, hemoglobinuria, metabolic acidosis, repetitive vomiting, hyperpyrexia).
d) IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 and 48 h (preferred; obtained in Canada through the Canadian Malaria Network), followed by a full oral course (e.g., atovaquone-proguanil) once able to take PO; parenteral quinine is the alternative.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ring haemorrhages as the classic cerebral-malaria neuropathology is standard WHO/pathology teaching; the text emphasizes sequestration/cytoadherence.

cohort_answer.text:
Parasetemia >5% in non-immune for >5yo; Hb <70; ARDS; Impaired conciousness
Sequestration of infected RBCs in brain microvasculature, ring haemorrhages
IV artesunate for at least 24 hours then complete therapy with a course of atovaquone-proguanil

questions.model_answer:

questions.question_raw: 29. Plasmodium knowlesi is a new species causing malaria in humans.

parts.text: Briefly describe how its morphology compares with other Plasmodium spp. on a blood smear.

Why is it important to distinguish this species from other non-falciparum species?

parts_raw.text: Shortly describe how its morphology compares with other Plasmodium spp. on a blood smear
b) Name the geographic region where most cases have been acquired
c) Why is it important to make the difference between this species and other non-falciparum species?

questions.model_answer:
a) On a thin film P. knowlesi is difficult to distinguish: early ring/trophozoite forms are indistinguishable from P. falciparum, while mature trophozoites, schizonts, band forms and gametocytes resemble P. malariae; infected red cells are normal-sized without Schuffner dots.
b) Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia (Malaysian Borneo).
c) Unlike P. malariae (72-h cycle), P. knowlesi replicates every 24 h, so parasitaemia rises rapidly and it can reach high parasitaemias and cause severe, life-threatening disease like P. falciparum; misreading it as benign P. malariae risks under-treatment and delayed recognition of deterioration.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific geographic region (Malaysia/Borneo) is established knowledge and referenced (Singh 2004) but not spelled out as a cite-able line in the text slice.

cohort_answer.text: Morphology: Early trophozoites resemble P. falciparum, later erythrocytic stages resemble P. malariae, making microscopy alone difficult. High parasitemias (replicates q24hr vs q3d for P. malariae); infects RBC of all ages; RBC diameter normal (vs big RBC in P. vivax/ovale); no ameboid trophozoites; band forms present (key for P. malariae/P. knowlesi); up to 16 merozoites. Region: SE Asia (Malaysia). Importance: P. knowlesi infections have higher parasitemias and can cause severe disease, similar to P. falciparum.

questions.model_answer:
a) Plasmodium falciparum.
b) Both India and Cambodia transmit falciparum and vivax, but P. falciparum is the species that characteristically causes severe malaria; breakthrough of severe disease despite mefloquine prophylaxis fits mefloquine-resistant P. falciparum.
c) Cambodia (Greater Mekong subregion of Southeast Asia), a region of documented mefloquine resistance.
d) First-line: IV artesunate. Second-line: IV quinine (or quinidine) plus doxycycline/clindamycin.
e) Artesunate clears parasitaemia faster and reduced mortality by ~22-35% versus quinine in randomized trials; it is safer and better tolerated, with less cardiotoxicity and hypoglycaemia and no need for continuous ECG monitoring.
f) Serial blood smears to measure parasite clearance (clearance half-life) — delayed clearance signals emerging artemisinin resistance (associated with K13 propeller mutations).

cohort_answer.text:
Species: P. falciparum
Why: Falciparum & vivax sp are found in both countries but falciparum is the only one that typically causes severe malaria. Known mefloquine resistance in Cambodia.
Place of acquisition: Cambodia (has areas of Mefloquine resistance)
Treatments: Parentral Artesunate; Parentral Quinine + clinda
Why first-line better: Rapid activity, clears parasitemia faster; Activity against all erythrocytic stages of the parasite; Minimal resistance; Very well tolerated, less adverse effects compared to quinine (eg hypoglycaemia); Easy to administer; No dose adjustment for organ impairment; No significant drug interactions; Does not require cardiac monitoring. Disadvantages: Short half life <2hrs therefore can relapse if not given an oral course as step down; Can cause delayed haemolysis (weekly CBCs x 4 weeks)
Monitoring resistance: Repeat blood smears to monitor clearance of parasitemia – if delayed, may have resistance

questions.question: For rapid diagnosis of malaria, list two advantages and two disadvantages each for blood smear, rapid diagnostic test (RDT), and PCR.

parts.text: For malaria rapid diagnosis, give 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for each of smear, RDT, and PCR.

parts_raw.text: Malaria for rapid diagnosis list the following (2 for each): advantage, disadvantage for smear, RDT, and PCR.

questions.model_answer:
a) Smear — Advantages: (1) allows speciation; (2) quantifies parasitaemia and monitors response to therapy. Disadvantages: (1) requires an experienced microscopist/technician; (2) can be falsely negative at low parasitaemia or when mature forms are sequestered.
RDT — Advantages: (1) rapid results; (2) useful where expert microscopy is delayed or unavailable (high sensitivity/specificity for P. falciparum). Disadvantages: (1) HRP-2 tests are limited to/most sensitive for P. falciparum and less sensitive for non-falciparum species; (2) remain positive up to 28 days after treatment so cannot monitor response (also false-negative at low density or with prozone effect).
PCR — Advantages: (1) high sensitivity and specificity, detects very low parasitaemias; (2) confirms species and mixed infections. Disadvantages: (1) not widely available; (2) expensive with slower turnaround.
questions.beyond_mandell: PCR advantages/disadvantages are general lab knowledge; the chapter only references PCR-confirmed diagnosis.

cohort_answer.text: Smear - Advantage: Allows for quantification and speciation. Disadvantage: Need a trained technician/hematopathologist to read/do smear; Can be false negative if low level parasitemia. RDT - Advantage: Rapid results. Disadvantage: Doesn't provide quantification of parasitemia; Doesn't identify all malaria species. PCR - Advantage: High sensitivity and specificity for identification, can detect low parasitemias. Disadvantage: Not widely available; Expensive

She was treated with 3 days of artemether-lumefantrine 10 days ago. Physician in community reorders RDT and smears. RDT returns positive. She is afebrile and well appearing and there was a smear with gametocytes of P. falciparum. Normal bw otherwise. No other plans to travel.

parts.text: Give 4 specific reasons why the RDT is positive.
What is the recommended management now?

parts_raw.text: 4 specific reasons why the RDT is positive
What is the recommended management now

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Persistent HRP-2 antigenaemia — HRP-2 RDTs stay positive up to ~28 days after successful treatment; (2) Circulating gametocytes — ACTs do not reliably clear mature P. falciparum gametocytes, which keep generating antigen/LDH signal; (3) Recrudescence/treatment failure (inadequate dose/absorption or resistance) with residual asexual parasites; (4) Re-infection with a new P. falciparum infection.
b) The smear shows only gametocytes (no asexual forms) in a well, afebrile child — this is residual gametocytaemia after successful cure, not active disease. Gametocytes are non-pathogenic and clear spontaneously, so no further antimalarial treatment is required; reassure and confirm absence of asexual parasitaemia. (A single low-dose primaquine is used only to block onward transmission in endemic settings — unnecessary here with no local transmission or further travel.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Gametocyte persistence after ACT and single-dose primaquine for transmission-blocking are WHO/CDC guidance, not detailed in this chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) Thin/thick smear - Advantages: accepted diagnostic standard; speciates and quantifies parasitemia (thick concentrates ~40x for detection, thin for speciation). questions.model_answer: a) P. vivax (and P. ovale) form dormant liver-stage hypnozoites; radical cure to prevent relapse requires an 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine or tafenoquine), and these are the only drugs active against hypnozoites. questions.model_answer: a) Advise deferring non-essential travel to this high-transmission, chloroquine-resistant area (West Africa) until after delivery if feasible. If travel proceeds, prescribe chemoprophylaxis: mefloquine is the drug of choice in pregnancy for chloroquine-resistant areas (reported safe/effective in 2nd/3rd trimesters and possibly 1st). Atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline are not recommended in pregnancy; chloroquine is ineffective due to resistance. Emphasize mosquito-avoidance measures (DEET, permethrin-treated clothing/bed nets) alongside prophylaxis, as no regimen is 100% effective. b) Treat as malaria until proven otherwise: urgent thick and thin Giemsa smears (repeat q12h if negative) +/- RDT for species and parasitemia; check CBC, glucose, renal function, lactate, and blood cultures. Hospitalize because pregnancy raises morbidity/mortality risk. If P. falciparum with any severity criterion, treat as severe malaria with IV artesunate (available in Canada via the Canadian Malaria Network), then complete oral therapy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Pregnant travelers advised to defer travel to high risk areas until after delivery if feasible. In this case mefloquine is the only ppx safe in pregnancy in Senegal (West Africa, known chloroquine-resistant malaria). questions.model_answer: a) He meets multiple WHO severe-malaria criteria: severe anemia (Hb 65 g/L), respiratory distress/hypoxemia (SaO2 85%), and cerebral malaria (diminished consciousness, GCS 9). Parasitemia 6% approaches hyperparasitemia. b) Sequestration of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes in the cerebral microvasculature (cytoadherence to endothelium), with ring hemorrhages, and postmortem parasite/pigment accumulation in cerebral vessels. c) Any four of: hyperparasitemia (>=500,000/uL, ~10%); hypoglycemia (glucose <=40 mg/dL); jaundice/hyperbilirubinemia; renal insufficiency; hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever); shock; metabolic acidosis; prostration; repetitive vomiting; hyperpyrexia; cessation of eating and drinking; seizures.

cohort_answer.text: B) Sequestration of infected erythrocytes in cerebral microvessels, 'ring' hemorrhages, perivascular leukocyte infiltrates, thrombin deposition, and activated platelets (Mandell's).

questions.question: A man returns from Africa with fever; a malaria rapid diagnostic test (HRP-2 assay) is negative.
questions.question_raw: Q14 (2009 PM). Malaria rapid detection test in a man who returns from Africa with fever. HRP assay is negative.

parts.text: Give 2 reasons for the (presumed false-negative) HRP-2 result.
The initial smear is read as negative. He returns and the smear now shows 1% falciparum parasitemia. Give TWO reasons why the initial smear was negative (other than laboratory error).

parts_raw.text: A) 2 reasons why (presumably false negative)
B) Initial smear read as negative. Returns again and smear now shows 1% parasitemia with falciparum. TWO reasons why the initial smear was negative (other than lab error)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) The P. falciparum strain does not express (or has deleted) HRP-2 antigen, giving a true HRP-2-negative result; (2) a prozone (high-dose hook) effect at very high antigen concentration blocks antibody binding and produces a false-negative. (Also: parasite density below the RDT limit of detection, ~100-1000/uL.) b) (1) Parasitemia below the microscopic limit of detection early in illness (parasitemia can lag symptoms by days); (2) sequestration of mature cytoadherent forms (trophozoites/schizonts) in the microvasculature so few parasites circulate on the initial smear.

cohort_answer.text: A) The prozone effect (high dose-hook phenomenon) - false-negative/false-low results due to excess antigens or antibodies, blocking binding sites of detection/capture antibodies. B) Initial parasitemia below level of detection; parasite life cycle - parasites synchronize and trophozoites/schizonts can be sequestered in microvasculature.

questions.question: Plasmodium knowlesi malaria.
questions.question_raw: Q15 (2014, 2009 AM). Malaria - P. knowlesi

parts.text: How does it compare to other malaria species on thin smear?
What geographic area is it found in?
Why is it relevant to distinguish it from other malaria species in the area?
How to identify it on smear?

parts_raw.text: A) How does it compare to other malaria species on thin smear?
B) What geographic area is it found?
C) Why is it relevant to distinguish it from other malaria species in the area?
D) How to identify on smear?

questions.model_answer: a) On thin smear P. knowlesi is morphologically indistinguishable from other species: its ring/early trophozoite forms resemble P. falciparum, while its mature forms, band-form trophozoites and gametocytes resemble P. malariae. b) Southeast Asia (the range of macaque reservoir hosts and Anopheles leucosphyrus-group vectors), especially Malaysian Borneo. c) Because it can behave far more aggressively than P. malariae: its erythrocytic cycle is only ~24 h, so parasitemia rises rapidly and daily fevers occur, and it can cause severe, life-threatening disease requiring prompt/parenteral treatment (unlike benign quartan P. malariae). d) Morphology alone is unreliable (overlaps P. malariae and P. falciparum); definitive identification requires molecular testing (species-specific PCR). Clues favouring knowlesi: high parasitemia, daily fever, and compatible SE Asian exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: PCR as the definitive identification method for P. knowlesi is standard reference-lab practice (CDC/WHO), noted only briefly in the chapter's speciation discussion.

cohort_answer.text: A) P. knowlesi looks like P. malariae (though can have daily fevers and high parasitemia with knowlesi vs low parasitemia and fever q3days with malariae); blood stage (band-form) schizont indistinguishable from P. malariae; early trophozoite (ring shape) identical to P. falciparum. B) Mainly southeast Asia, majority from Malaysian Borneo; also Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, southern China, Vietnam, Laos, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Andaman islands (India), Kalimantan, Sumatra, Indonesia - follows distribution of macaque hosts and Anopheles leucosphyrus vector. C) Associated with fatalities with delayed treatment; erythrocyte phase lasts 24h (shortest of any human malaria species), can develop daily fever spikes and rapid high parasitemia; severe disease in 6-9% of symptomatic adults.

questions.question: Define the endemic regions for Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi, and identify the malaria species found in Papua New Guinea.
questions.question_raw: Q16 (2014). Malaria - define the endemic regions for: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi. What kind of malaria is in Papua New Guinea?

parts.text: Define the endemic regions and identify the malaria species in Papua New Guinea.

parts_raw.text: Define the endemic regions and identify the malaria species in Papua New Guinea

questions.model_answer: P. falciparum: widespread in nearly all endemic areas - sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Oceania/Papua New Guinea, and parts of South America; chloroquine resistance is widespread. P. vivax: Americas, Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, western Pacific/Oceania, and (less commonly) sub-Saharan Africa - relatively rare in West/Central Africa because of the Duffy-negative phenotype. P. ovale: mainly sub-Saharan (especially West) Africa, and parts of Asia. P. malariae: sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia/Indonesia, western Pacific, and the Amazon basin. P. knowlesi: Southeast Asia (macaque distribution). Papua New Guinea: P. falciparum and P. vivax predominate, and both are notable for chloroquine resistance (high-grade chloroquine-resistant P. vivax is reported in Papua New Guinea and Indonesia).
questions.beyond_mandell: Precise species distributions (ovale mainly West Africa, vivax sparing Duffy-negative Africa, malariae range) rest on CDC/WHO epidemiology; the chapter names the resistance geography explicitly but the full species maps are standard reference knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: P. falciparum - widespread in nearly all malaria endemic areas: Sub-Saharan Africa, SE Asia/Papua New Guinea, upper South America (esp DR, Haiti), Oceania. P. vivax - Americas, West Pacific (Australia, New Guinea), Sub-Saharan Africa, India, SE Asia, upper South America (rare in central/western Africa due to Duffy negative phenotype); Florida and Texas recently locally acquired cases. P. ovale - Sub-Saharan Africa (esp west Africa) and Asia. P. malariae - sub-Saharan Africa, SE Asia, Indonesia, western Pacific islands, Amazon basin of S. America. P. knowlesi - SE Asia. Papua New Guinea: P. falciparum and P. vivax, chloroquine resistant (including P. vivax), mefloquine resistance.

questions.question: Why do you need to test for G6PD in Plasmodium vivax infection?

parts.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in Plasmodium vivax infection?

parts_raw.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in P. vivax infection?

questions.model_answer: P. vivax (and P. ovale) produce dormant liver hypnozoites; after blood-stage treatment (e.g. chloroquine, which is inactive against hypnozoites), radical cure to prevent relapse requires an 8-aminoquinoline - primaquine or tafenoquine. Both cause dose-dependent oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, which can be massive and fatal in severe (e.g. Mediterranean-type) deficiency, so they are contraindicated there. G6PD activity must therefore be documented before prescribing; with mild/borderline deficiency, weekly primaquine (e.g. 45 mg base weekly x 8 weeks) may be used with monitoring. Primaquine and tafenoquine are also contraindicated in pregnancy because fetal G6PD status cannot be assessed.

cohort_answer.text: P. vivax, P. ovale, or P. malariae infections require treatment of dormant hypnozoite liver stages with primaquine or tafenoquine to prevent relapse; both can cause oxidant hemolysis if G6PD deficient. Severe G6PD deficiency (5-10% normal activity): primaquine should not be used. ~20% G6PD activity: primaquine can be used at 0.75mg/kg qweekly x6 weeks, stop if significant hemolysis. Primaquine cannot be used in pregnancy because fetal G6PD status unknown.

questions.question: A woman travels to Africa without taking malaria prophylaxis and now has a decreased level of consciousness; the blood film shows Plasmodium falciparum.
questions.question_raw: Q20 (2003 PM). Woman travels to Africa, doesn't take malaria ppx. Now has decreased LOC, blood film showing P. falciparum

parts.text: How would you treat this patient?
What are 5 signs of severe Plasmodium falciparum infection?
What adjunctive therapy can you suggest?

parts_raw.text: A) How would you treat this patient?
B) What are 5 signs of severe P. falciparum infection?
C) What adjunctive therapy can you suggest?

questions.model_answer: a) This is severe (cerebral) malaria - a medical emergency. Give IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (children <20 kg: 3 mg/kg) at 0, 12, 24 and 48 h (preferred treatment; in Canada via the Canadian Malaria Network), managed in ICU. After clinical improvement/ability to tolerate oral, complete a full oral course with atovaquone-proguanil, artemether-lumefantrine, or quinine plus doxycycline (clindamycin if pregnant/child <8 y). b) Any five of: cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness/seizures); respiratory distress/acidosis; severe anemia; hypoglycemia; jaundice; renal insufficiency; hemoglobinuria; shock; hyperparasitemia (~>=10%); prostration; repetitive vomiting; hyperpyrexia. c) Supportive/adjunctive care: ICU monitoring; treat and monitor hypoglycemia (glucose q4-6h, dextrose infusions); careful fluid management (avoid over-resuscitation/pulmonary edema in adults); respiratory support; control seizures (benzodiazepines); transfuse for severe anemia; broad-spectrum antibiotics with cultures for possible concurrent bacteremia/sepsis. Exchange transfusion is no longer recommended by the CDC.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort suggests exchange transfusion may be considered at >10% parasitemia; the chapter states exchange transfusion is no longer CDC-recommended and of unproven/possibly harmful benefit.

cohort_answer.text: A) Parenteral Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (children <20kg: 3mg/kg) IV bolus over 1-2 min at 0, 12, 24, 48h; switch to oral follow-on after 24h if possible (if not, continue daily IV artesunate up to 7 days total); follow-on oral therapy starting 4h after final dose: Atovaquone-proguanil (adults 4 tabs daily x3 days with fatty food; peds 20mg/kg atovaquone + 8mg/kg proguanil daily x3 days) OR Doxycycline plus quinine sulphate OR Clindamycin (if unable to take doxy or atovaquone-proguanil) plus quinine sulphate. C) Supportive care; monitor BG q4h; respiratory support; treat seizures (benzos first line); fluid requirements target CVP 2-5cm (include dextrose); transfuse to target Hb>70 (>50 in high risk settings); manage concomitant bacterial infections; exchange transfusion can be considered if parasitemia >10% per CATMAT.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman, 6 weeks pregnant, is travelling to India; she later returns with fevers and chills and a blood smear is shown [image-based question: peripheral smear, likely falciparum with a vivax-like trophozoite].
questions.question_raw: Q21 (2006 PM). 23F 6 weeks pregnant, travelling to India.

parts.text: What malaria prophylaxis do you recommend?
She returns with fevers/chills; what does the smear show and how would you treat this infection?

parts_raw.text: A) What malaria ppx do you recommend?

B) She returns from her trip with fevers/chills etc. What does the smear show (there is a picture of a smear, it was probably falciparum although there was a troph that looked rather vivax-like). How would you treat this infection?

questions.model_answer: a) Mefloquine is the recommended prophylaxis in pregnancy for chloroquine-resistant India; advise deferring travel if feasible. Cannot use in pregnancy: atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, primaquine, tafenoquine; chloroquine is ineffective due to resistance. Add mosquito-avoidance measures. b) The smear shows P. falciparum (delicate rings/accolade and signet-ring forms, banana-shaped gametocytes, absence of mature forms). Treatment: if severe, IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, 48 h then a full oral course; in pregnancy use clindamycin + quinine (or artemether-lumefantrine in 2nd/3rd trimester). If uncomplicated, artemether-lumefantrine (2nd/3rd trimester) or quinine + clindamycin. Avoid halofantrine, primaquine and tetracyclines throughout pregnancy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Drugs usable in pregnancy: Chloroquine (but resistance in India), Mefloquine. Cannot use: Primaquine, Tafenoquine, Malarone, Doxycycline. Answer given as: Mefloquine; advise against travel. B) If severe: Artesunate IV followed by artemether/lumefantrine (Coartem) or clindamycin. If uncomplicated: PO artesunate 4mg/kg daily x3 days + mefloquine 25mg/kg; Artemether-lumefantrine BID x3 days with food; Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine daily x3 days; Quinine TID + clindamycin BID x7 days. Avoid artemisinin/derivatives in 1st trimester; avoid halofantrine, primaquine, tetracycline at all times in pregnancy; avoid sulfadoxine near term; not enough evidence for malarone or coartem in pregnancy.

questions.question: List 3 medications that can be used for malaria prophylaxis in sub-Saharan Africa; indicate dose, route, frequency, and one contraindication (excluding hypersensitivity).

parts.text: List 3 medications which can be used for malaria prophylaxis in sub-Saharan Africa. Indicate dose, route, frequency and a contraindication (excluding hypersensitivity).

parts_raw.text: List 3 medications which can be used for malaria ppx in sub-Saharan Africa. Indicate dose, route, frequency and a contraindication (excluding hypersensitivity)

questions.model_answer: (1) Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 1 adult tablet (250/100 mg) PO daily, starting 1-2 days before travel through 7 days after leaving; contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30), and not recommended in pregnancy or children <5 kg. (2) Doxycycline 100 mg PO daily, starting 1-2 days before travel through 4 weeks after leaving; contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding and children <8 years. (3) Mefloquine 250 mg (salt) PO once weekly, starting 2-3 weeks before travel through 4 weeks after leaving; contraindicated in cardiac conduction abnormalities, seizure history, or serious neuropsychiatric illness. (Chloroquine is NOT usable - widespread resistance in sub-Saharan Africa.)

cohort_answer.text: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 250/100mg PO daily begin 1-2 days before travel until 7 days post-travel; contraindications: pregnancy, children <5kg, breastfeeding, CrCl<30. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily 1-2 days before travel until 4 weeks after return; contraindications: pregnancy, children <8 years. Mefloquine 250mg PO weekly from 2-3 weeks before travel until 4 weeks after; contraindications: hx seizures, psychiatric hx, cardiac conduction abnormalities; resistance at Thailand-Cambodian border and parts of China, Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos. Note tafenoquine avoid in pregnancy, psychiatric conditions, G6PD deficiency. Avoid chloroquine (high resistance in Africa).

questions.question: Malaria chemoprophylaxis for travelers to Honduras.
questions.question_raw: Q23 (2017 AM). Malaria ppx for travelers to Honduras

parts.text: Name four regimens. When is each drug started and when is it stopped?

parts_raw.text: Name 4 regimens. When to start and when to stop each drug?

questions.model_answer: Honduras lies in Central America west of the Panama Canal, an area WITHOUT chloroquine resistance, so chloroquine is an option. Four regimens (per CDC/Mandell chemoprophylaxis table): (1) Chloroquine phosphate 300 mg base PO once weekly, begin 1-2 weeks before travel, continue weekly for 4 weeks after leaving. (2) Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 1 adult tablet PO daily, begin 1-2 days before travel, continue daily for 7 days after leaving. (3) Doxycycline 100 mg PO daily, begin 1-2 days before travel, continue daily for 4 weeks after leaving. (4) Mefloquine 250 mg salt PO once weekly, begin 2-3 weeks before travel, continue weekly for 4 weeks after leaving. (Primaquine 30 mg base daily, 1-2 days before to 7 days after, is an alternative in predominantly P. vivax areas if G6PD normal.)

cohort_answer.text: No resistance in Honduras. Malarone 250/100mg PO daily from 1-2 days before until 7 days after return. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily from 1-2 days before until 4 weeks after returning. Mefloquine 250mg salt PO weekly 3 weeks before until 4 weeks after returning. Primaquine 30mg PO daily from day 1 before to 7d after exposure (check G6PD first). Chloroquine 500mg salt PO weekly 1-2 weeks before until 4 weeks after travel (chloroquine sensitive areas: Mexico, Central America west of Panama Canal, Haiti, DR, Middle East - P. vivax, ovale, malariae, knowlesi). Tafenoquine begin daily x3 days prior (loading dose), weekly during travel, and 7 days after leaving.

questions.model_answer: a) Any three WHO severe-malaria features present here (Table 274.1): (1) cerebral malaria / diminished consciousness (altered LOC); (2) respiratory distress (tachypnea, dyspnea, crackles); (3) renal insufficiency (renal dysfunction). Severe anemia is a further qualifying feature. b) (1) First line: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 and 48 h (preferred treatment for severe malaria). (2) Alternative: IV quinine dihydrochloride 20 mg/kg loading dose over 4 h, then 10 mg/kg over 3-4 h every 8 h (or IV quinidine gluconate where artesunate/quinine unavailable). c) After parenteral artemisinin, complete cure with an oral agent to prevent recrudescence: doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days (alternatives: atovaquone-proguanil, clindamycin, or mefloquine).

cohort_answer.text: A) Altered LOC; Respiratory distress; Anemia (Hct<15%?); AKI (Cr>250?). B) First Line: Artesunate IV 2.4mg/kg/dose at 0,12,24,48h. Alternate: Quinine IV loading dose 20mg/kg over 4h then 10mg/kg q8h. C) Artemisinin-based combination tx (artemether-lumefantrine) x3 days; Malarone (atovaquone/proguanil) with food 4 tabs daily x3 days; preferred oral regimens after ACT by WHO: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7days + quinine, or Clindamycin 20mg/kg/day PO div TID x7 days + quinine.

questions.model_answer: a) Four features met (Table 274.1): (1) cerebral malaria / diminished consciousness (GCS 9); (2) respiratory distress (RR 30); (3) hypoxemia/pulmonary involvement (SpO2 85%); (4) hyperparasitemia (6%). b) Four other criteria: (1) severe anemia; (2) hypoglycemia; (3) jaundice/icterus; (4) renal insufficiency (others: prostration, hemoglobinuria, shock, repetitive vomiting, hyperpyrexia, seizures). c) Dense sequestration of parasitized (infected) erythrocytes within the cerebral microvasculature. d) IV (parenteral) artesunate. e) Yes. Artemisinins produce rapid parasite clearance (clinical improvement usually within 24-36 h); a fall from 2% to 1% with a downward trend by day 3 is an adequate response, after which therapy is completed orally.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parasitemia threshold: Mandell/WHO define endemic hyperparasitemia as ~10% (500,000/uL), but CDC counts parasitemia >=5% as a severe-malaria criterion in nonimmune travelers, and CDC advises continuing daily IV artesunate up to 7 days until parasitemia <=1% before switching to oral therapy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Altered LOC; Parasitemia >5%; Respiratory distress; (not enough info given for 4th criterion). C) Dense sequestration of parasitized pRBC in CNS capillaries. D) IV Artesunate. E) Yes - after artemisinin tx, parasitemia clearance should be seen by day 5; if 1% by day 3 that is an adequate response; 6% likely underestimate given sequestration so 1% is a very good response. CDC: if after third IV artesunate dose parasite density >1%, continue IV artesunate once daily up to 7 days until density <=1%, then switch to oral regimen.

questions.model_answer: a) Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) - classic prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia, with an incubation of months. b) Demonstration of amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) on splenic aspirate (highest sensitivity) or bone marrow aspirate, with Giemsa stain and/or culture and PCR; rK39 serology supports the diagnosis. c) Leishmania donovani (the agent of visceral leishmaniasis on the Indian subcontinent). d) Liposomal amphotericin B (first-line and the only FDA-approved agent for this indication): e.g., 3 mg/kg on days 1-5, 14, and 21.

questions.question: A patient returns from southern Africa where malaria was diagnosed and treated with artemether-lumefantrine. The family doctor notes a positive rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Creatinine and liver function tests are normal.
questions.question_raw: A patient returns from somewhere in Southern Africa. He was diagnosed with malaria while away and received Artemether-Lumefantrine. His family doctor notes a positive RDT. Creatinine and LFTs are normal.

parts.text: List four reasons why the RDT is positive.
A blood smear shows gametocytes on 2 of 3 smears. Do you treat, and why?
List two recommended first-line regimens if the patient is returning from Malawi for uncomplicated falciparum malaria.

parts_raw.text: List 4 reasons why the RDT is positive.
A blood smear shows gametocytes on 2 of 3 smears. Do you treat and why?
2 recommended first line regimens if patient returning from Malawi for uncomplicated falciparum.

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons: (1) HRP-2-based RDTs remain persistently positive for up to ~4 weeks (28 days) after treatment, even when the patient is cured; (2) persistence of circulating gametocytes (not cleared by schizonticides); (3) treatment failure or re-infection with ongoing parasitemia; (4) false positive from cross-reacting antibodies (e.g., rheumatoid factor) or another infection. b) No. Gametocytes are the non-pathogenic sexual stage and do not cause clinical (asexual-stage) illness; asymptomatic gametocytemia after adequate ACT does not warrant re-treatment. A single gametocytocidal dose of primaquine may be considered only for transmission-blocking where competent Anopheles vectors are present. c) Malawi has chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum, so two first-line regimens are: (1) artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem); (2) atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone). Quinine plus doxycycline (or clindamycin) is an alternative.
questions.beyond_mandell: Persistence of gametocytes, cross-reacting rheumatoid factor as an RDT false positive, and single-dose primaquine for transmission blocking are drawn from CDC/WHO malaria guidance rather than explicit statements in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Reasons for positive RDT: Persistence of gametocytes; persistent positive even after successful treatment (antibody-based can be positive ~30-60d post-treatment); re-infection or treatment failure; auto antibodies (RF); other non-plasmodium infection (African trypanosomiasis, toxo, TB, dengue). Gametocytes: No, do not treat - gametocytes will not cause symptoms; can consider treatment if in area with Anopheles mosquito to prevent disease introduction. First line regimens: Atovaquone-Proguanil (Malarone); Quinine + Clindamycin or Doxycycline.

questions.model_answer:
a) TB meningitis: Yes (adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality; ATS/IDSA/WHO).
b) Neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst: Yes, co-administered with antiparasitic therapy to blunt the inflammatory reaction (IDSA/ASTMH NCC guidelines); not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema.
c) Cerebral malaria: No (corticosteroids are associated with worse outcomes/prolonged coma; contraindicated).
d) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome/neuroschistosomiasis): Yes (corticosteroids before/with praziquantel; CDC/UpToDate).
e) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: No (risk of anaphylaxis is managed with peri-procedural antihistamines and anaphylaxis readiness plus concomitant albendazole, not adjunctive steroids).
questions.beyond_mandell: These topics (TB meningitis, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis) are outside the Acute Meningitis chapter; answers rest on IDSA/ASTMH, WHO malaria, and CDC parasitic-disease guidance.

questions.model_answer: (1) TB meningitis: YES - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in confirmed TBM (not HIV+, where evidence is weaker). Note: steroids are NOT routine during purely empirical/diagnostic therapy as they blunt the clinical and CSF response and can worsen an undiagnosed fungal infection. (2) Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst: YES - corticosteroids control the peri-lesional inflammation/edema provoked by antiparasitic (albendazole) therapy; not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated edema. (3) Cerebral malaria: NO - randomized data show steroids are harmful (prolonged coma, more complications). (4) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama / acute neuroschistosomiasis): YES - corticosteroids given with praziquantel to suppress the hypersensitivity reaction. (5) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: NO - no role for adjunctive steroids; risk is anaphylaxis, managed with antihistamines/epinephrine and peri-procedural albendazole, not steroids.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the TB-meningitis point is touched in this chapter (p. 1225, advising against routine steroids during empirical therapy). Steroid use in confirmed TBM, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, and echinococcosis/PAIR rests on IDSA/WHO guidance and the respective Mandell disease chapters, not the chronic meningitis chapter.
